skript.thema: Claude Code: handing over what it can't see

teile.name: Hook
teile.text: Some project knowledge lives only in someone's head. Claude Code can't see that, so what should you hand over?
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: black-haired man in black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses frowns thoughtfully at a cluttered desk of tangled cables in a dim home office, medium shot, cool lamp light.

teile.name: Unseen info
teile.text: The docs say Claude reads your code well. But a deploy process in someone's head isn't in the repo.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: a thoughtful programmer in a rainy window-lit office taps their temple while streaks of light reflect on their glasses, close-up, warm and cool contrast.

teile.name: Write it down
teile.text: So what goes in your handover? Only what Claude can't find by reading the repo. Skip the rest.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter in leather jacket and cyan glasses writes a short list on a board, seen over his shoulder, medium shot, soft desk lamp light.

teile.name: Examples
teile.text: The docs' examples: a meeting decision, a deploy process, an environment variable tests need.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: three colleagues around a meeting table, one gesturing while explaining a decision, others nodding, wide shot, warm office light, no screens or papers visible.

teile.name: Check
teile.text: Give it a check to run. Without one, the docs say, Claude may say it's done too early.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: presenter with cyan glasses leans toward a laptop seen from the side, eyebrows raised as a green glow lights his face, close shot, dark workshop background.

teile.name: Cost
teile.text: Claude Code comes with Pro, listed at $20 if billed monthly. Usage limits apply.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the presenter sits at a cafe table, calmly sipping coffee while considering a decision, expressive face, medium shot, golden evening light, no screens visible.

teile.name: Ending
teile.text: The knowledge from someone's head now sits in a note Claude can read. Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: presenter in black leather jacket and cyan glasses smiles with relief, the once-tangled cables now neatly bundled on the desk behind him, medium shot, warm light.

regeln: Within each spoken phase use multiple distinct relevant shots, roughly 3-5 seconds each for Shorts; long videos can allow purposeful longer demonstrations. Preserve continuous narration and accurate subtitle timing.
A zoom, crop, subtitle change or decorative background does not count as a new motif. Never fill missing images with candles, unrelated stock or background-only frames.
Show the main image prominently; avoid tiny repeated photos in a mostly empty vertical frame. Preserve genuine evidence and important image details.
For AI Tools Explained identify the exact tool briefly, then show genuine interface views and different source-supported examples. Never present stock or an illustration as a real tool result.
Use original urban painted open-world-game poster styling for fictional scenes and presenters; no copied game characters. Match narrated action and era.

Clear speech and readable captions alone do not make a professional video. Inspect useful motif changes and narration-image alignment over the entire video. Missing main imagery is a substantial defect.
Include mandatory spoken like, share and save calls at the correct format-specific positions. Do not replace this requirement with a different CTA.

AI Tools Explained is for viewers with a practical task. Do not read parameter counts, architecture names, pipeline tags, context lengths or benchmark claims as a substitute for useful explanation. Explain the human task, the source-supported action and a concrete limit. A generic trending-tools question failed story review twice; prefer a specific visual workflow.

The user confirmed original presenter references on 2026-10-05: Business Origin Stories uses the blue-eyed man with a fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch; AI Tools Explained uses the black-haired man with black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses. Preserve identity and typical clothing, vary action and setting.

Introduce the correct presenter at the opening and bring that same presenter back during the video in useful actions. Do not confine the figure to the ending. Do not replace original channel figures with different fictional people; anonymous period workers remain clearly illustrative supporting people, never a real-founder likeness.

Prefer vivid original painted open-world-game scenes to long holds on lifeless documentary photos. Preserve factual accuracy and show authentic tool examples briefly as evidence. Camera moves alone are not new motifs or full character animation.

The user confirmed on 2026-10-05 that both new delivered videos are much better than before. Preserve the original painted world, recurring channel identity, matching main imagery, music and useful scene changes. The long-term quality target remains 10/10; the user did not give these videos a numeric score. Do not replace their actual AI scores or the existing 7/10 delivery threshold with the aspirational target.

Start immediately with the specific tool name and a concrete promise or subject within the first 3 seconds; avoid generic openings or abstract premises.
Introduce a new, actionable insight or concrete step with each line, focusing on human tasks rather than abstract specs, architecture names, or benchmark numbers.

belege.name: Claude Code official guide
belege.text:
Official Claude Code documentation/help page.
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Best practices for Claude Code - Claude Code Docs
Fetch the complete documentation index at: /docs/llms.txt
Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
Claude Code is built in a way that, in most cases, your first plain prompt in a fresh session already does the right thing, without any setup on your part.
To let commands run safely without you approving each one, new terminal and VS Code sessions start in auto mode , where a classifier reviews anything risky before it runs.
To keep your main conversation focused while independent work happens in parallel, Claude delegates to subagents and checks in only when it has to.
To keep a long session going without you managing it, your conversation is compacted automatically before the context window fills.
This page covers what to do when the defaults aren’t enough. That usually happens when your project has knowledge, rules, or constraints that Claude can’t see from the code alone:
A deploy process that lives in someone’s head
A file that must never be read
A check that has to pass before anything counts as done
A budget you need to stay under
No default can know those things about your project, so this is where a small amount of setup on your side pays off.
When a session doesn’t go the way you expected, it’s almost always one of these:
Claude built something different from what you had in mind, or it has to rediscover the same fact at the start of every session. It’s missing information it can’t get from reading the repo. See Tell Claude what it can’t see .
Claude said it was done and it wasn’t quite, usually because it had no way to check its own work. See Give Claude a check to run .
Claude did something that must never happen in this repo, or skipped a step that must always happen. A prompt alone can’t guarantee either of those. See Enforce the rules that can’t have exceptions .
Claude got it right, but it took more time, tokens, or permission prompts than the task was worth. See Change a default .
Let Claude run without you applies the same four points to unattended runs, and What you can stop doing lists the advice that current models have made unnecessary.
Setup for a whole team is on a separate page: Set up Claude Code for your organization .
Every instruction you give Claude Code is one of these:
Non-deterministic: you write the instruction, and Claude (the model) reads it. This can be your prompt, CLAUDE.md , or a skill. The model then decides what to do with this information. It usually follows your commands, and current models are good at understanding your intent without much context, but there’s no guarantee that it’ll follow your instructions. It can still decide not to do things, or do other things.
Deterministic: you configure the instruction, and Claude Code (the harness) has to execute this. This can be a hook, a deny rule, or a managed setting. Claude Code applies this every time, no matter what the model decided to do.
Most things in Claude Code come in both forms:
Non-deterministic (Claude decides) Deterministic (Claude Code enforces)
What to do Your prompt, CLAUDE.md , skills Claude picks up itself Hooks, and which skills only you can start
What it can touch Auto mode’s classifier Deny rules, the sandbox in strict mode , managed settings
When it’s done A request for evidence, /goal , /code-review Tests, typecheck, a Stop hook, CI
How much it spends Effort level, Claude’s own pace --max-turns or --max-budget-usd with -p , a spend limit you’ve set
Who has the last word Claude’s summary of what it did Branch protection, a person who approves the merge
Most of the time, you want Claude to decide. Almost every guideline has exceptions, and current models are good at reading the code in front of them and judging whether a guideline fits the situation. With the actual code in front of it, Claude is usually better placed to make that call than a rule you wrote in advance.
The deterministic kind is for when you want to make sure certain things always happen (or never happen), no matter what the model decides. This doesn’t have to be anything dramatic. Auto mode already blocks the dramatic things , like a production deploy or a force push over someone’s work. It’s usually something specific to your project, and it can be as niche as you want it to be:
Never edit the generated client in src/gen/
Always run the license-header script after creating a file
You could’ve written either of these as a line in CLAUDE.md or in your prompt, and Claude would follow it nearly every time. But no matter how strongly you word it, whether Claude follows that line on a given turn is still Claude’s call.
If you keep adding emphasis to a CLAUDE.md line and Claude still misses it, that’s a sign the line belongs in a hook. The reverse holds too: if you have hooks for things that are only preferences, delete them and let Claude decide.
Tell Claude what it can’t see
Only write down what Claude can’t find by reading the repo, or what it would otherwise spend time rediscovering every session.
Claude starts every task by reading your code, and current models are very good at this. They’ll find your file layout, your conventions, your test framework, and how existing components are built, usually faster than you could explain them. That means Claude already knows most of what you might be tempted to write down for it.
What it can’t find is the information that was never in the repo:
A decision your team made in a meeting
A deploy process that lives in one person’s head
The environment variable your integration tests need
There’s also information that is in the repo but takes a few minutes of digging to find, and Claude has to redo that digging at the start of every session.
A good test before you write anything down for Claude:
Could it find this by reading the code?
Would it actually go and look?
If both are yes, leave it out.
A specific prompt helps for the same reason, because it gives Claude information it doesn’t already hav
